title: burst-spline-sensitivity-session-econ-bench
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a compact bench experiment exploring how short, high-cardinality microbursts ('burst-spline' patterns) interact with sessionized request mixes. Goal: quantify latency percentile shifts and cost delta across three runtime strategies (baseline multiplexing, predictive-prefetch, slot-tiling) and produce a low-friction ASCII-style collateral that product and SRE can use in synopses.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Workload: session-heavy chat traffic with 60% short-turns (<32 tokens) and 40% long-turns (>=128 tokens), bursty arrival pattern (poisson with occasional 3s microbursts).
- Compared configs: baseline (dyn-multiplex), predictive-prefetch (KV priming + lightweight prefetch), tiling (fixed slot tiling for microbursts).
- Outcome: predictive-prefetch reduces p50/p90 in microbursts with modest cost (approx +6% $/Q), tiling reduces p99 tail but increases baseline cost (+18% $/Q) and hurts sustained throughput. Baseline is best for balanced sustained workloads.

Experiment setup (short):
- Cluster: dev-gpu-pool-3 (A100 equivilent), 8-way nodes, 6 nodes used for this run. 1024 max concurrent slots.
- Model: open-llama-7b trimmed variant (seq-len 1024, KV friendly quant profile q4_0).
- Client mix: 10k simulated sessions, session lengths sampled from production session histogram (derived from tracewalk: cohort B). Burst injection every 120s window (burst amplitude 2.8x baseline for 3s).
- Metrics captured: p50/p90/p99 latency (server-side), tokens/sec, tokens-per-dollar (estimated from infra-hourly), cold-start count, KV cache hit-ratio.

Profiles tested:
1) baseline-multiplex: continuous multiplex+dynamic batching, opportunistic prefetch disabled.
2) predictive-prefetch: prefix-aware KV priming using 2000-pattern microprofile heuristic; prefetch window 150ms; cache TTL 30s.
3) tiling-fixed: fixed slot tiling with 8-slot tiles and reservation for microburst cohort; opportunistic tiling when microburst flag set.

Key numbers (median across 5 runs, bootstrapped):
- Baseline-multiplex:
  p50: 42 ms
  p90: 120 ms
  p99: 420 ms
  tokens/sec (sustained): 92k
  est $/1k queries: $0.78
  KV hit ratio: 31%

- Predictive-prefetch:
  p50: 36 ms (−14%)
  p90: 95 ms (−21%)
  p99: 360 ms (−14%)
  tokens/sec (sustained): 86k (−6%)
  est $/1k queries: $0.83 (+6%)
  KV hit ratio: 57%

- Tiling-fixed:
  p50: 44 ms (+5%)
  p90: 110 ms (−8%)
  p99: 260 ms (−38%)
  tokens/sec (sustained): 71k (−23%)
  est $/1k queries: $0.92 (+18%)
  KV hit ratio: 65%

Interpretation notes:
- Predictive-prefetch wins for median and middle-tail improvements at modest cost — it reduces the number of tokens spent on re-computation by priming KV entries for high-probability continuations. The throughput hit (~6%) is because prefetch consumes small amounts of GPU cycles/slots during non-burst times.
- Tiling-fixed dramatically improves p99 by isolating tail noise (reserved tiles avoid contention) but the reservation means underutilized cycles outside bursts, which reduces sustained throughput and raises $/Q. This is acceptable for high-SLA customers but poor for cost-sensitive hosted tenants.
- Baseline remains competitive overall for steady state; however, in dense microburst scenarios p90/p99 drift high.

ASCII charts (burst window focus, normalized to baseline p50=1.0):
Latency multipliers over burst (time in seconds, 0 is burst start):
Time(s) | Baseline | Prefetch | Tiling
-------------------------------------
-1.0    |   0.98   |   0.95   | 0.99
 0.0    |   1.65   |   1.20   | 1.12
 0.5    |   2.10   |   1.05   | 1.03
 1.0    |   1.85   |   0.98   | 0.90
 2.0    |   1.30   |   0.95   | 0.88
 4.0    |   1.05   |   0.96   | 0.95

Simple sparkline for p99 across configs (lower is better):
Baseline:  ▂▁▁▃▅████▇▆▇▆ (peak at burst)
Prefetch:  ▂▁▁▂▃███▅▃▂▂
Tiling:    ▁▁▁▁▁▃▇█▆▅▃  (steady and capped)

Cost sensitivity table (approx % change vs baseline):
Scenario          | Prefetch | Tiling
-----------------------------------
Low burst freqs   | +2%      | +6%
Medium (our test) | +6%      | +18%
High burst density| +12%     | +27%

Free-form observations:
- KV hit ratio correlates strongly with p50/p90 improvement; when hit-ratio >50%, prefetch returns strong median gains.
- Tiling is brittle if burst cohort misclassification occurs: when we incorrectly reserve tiles for non-burst sessions, cost/throughput hit becomes severe. See run #4 where misclassification spiked under synthetic skew.
- Cold-starts were rare (<0.2% across runs) because session stickiness + warm pools were used; if on-demand auto-scale was enabled cold penalty increases p99 significantly.

Guidance for product/ops:
- Hosted API (cost-sensitive): default to baseline-multiplex with predictive-prefetch off by default, opt-in for customers via flag when they want median/p90 improvements. Consider an automated prefetch advisory in Redwood Optimize that turns on prefetch when KV hit ratio historical >45%.
- Dedicated (SLA customers): offer tiled-reservation profile as a dedicated SKU with explicit pricing; call out p99 guarantees and throughput tradeoffs. Provide a canary/test endpoint to measure misclassification risk before full enablement.
- Console: add a sessionized curve visualization for the customer that overlays KV hit ratio and predicted prefetch ROI over time — this will make automated recommendations more trusted.

Open questions / next steps:
- Can we combine tiling with elastic reservation (grow/shrink tiles fast) to get p99 benefits without sustained cost hit? (Prototype: dynamic-tile-size control loop).
- How sensitive are results to model family? Repeat with a 70B trimmed variant and a quantized 3B to see scaling behaviour (tickets created).
- Add a heartbeat for prefetch efficacy in telemetry so Optimize can auto-toggle strategies per-tenant.

Notes to self / low-fi TODOs:
- Attach raw CSVs to INF-3421 and include run scripts in bench repo (PR linked above).
- Run the same workload with network egress latency +10ms to mimic edge customers.
- Draft a short one-pager for Sales describing tiling as an "ultra-tail protection" add-on.
